transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-09
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Liam Patel (Redwood AE), Riley Gomez (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Redwood Product), Priya Kapoor (Arsenal VP Product), Jorge Mendes (Arsenal Head of ML), Aisha Rahman (Eng Manager), Tom Boyle (SRE), Lina Park (Security)

Summary:
Quick product walkthrough focused on Redwood model catalog + compatibility matrix, how we pick open models, what bench artifacts we produce, and a roadmap to a pilot to validate latency/cost for Arsenal's QA/assist workload. Security and VPC/KMS questions surfaced; we covered hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs and proposed next steps for a 2-hr pilot run.

Topics:
- Catalog matchmaking and compatibility heuristics
- Bench methodology: latency, token-cost, accuracy proxies
- Runtime fit: quantization, kernel mapping, batching, caching
- Deployment options: Redwood API (hosted), Dedicated, Private (VPC)
- Security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM, audit logs

Action items: see metadata list above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Liam Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, we'll keep this fairly pragmatic. I'm Liam, I'm the AE on this account. With me is Riley, our solutions engineer, and Maya from product. Could you do quick intros from Arsenal?
[00:12] Priya Kapoor: Hi all, Priya here — VP Product at Arsenal Dynamics. We're looking to add a model catalog layer to standardize model selection across teams. Jorge will cover ML specifics.
[00:20] Jorge Mendes: Jorge, Head of ML. Our main use-cases are a QA-assistant and a short-form summarization microservice. Latency around 200ms p95 is our target for the assistant.
[00:30] Aisha Rahman: Aisha, engineering manager for the AI infra team. We'll be owning deployments if we go dedicated or private.
[00:35] Liam Patel: Great. Quick agenda: 1) Walk through the catalog + how we score models, 2) bench artifacts and compatibility matrix you'll get, 3) runtime fit and deployment options, 4) security questions and next steps.
[00:45] Riley Gomez: Quick one: when you say 200ms p95, is that for single-token latency or end-to-end?
[00:50] Jorge Mendes: End-to-end from API to response for medium length prompts (about 150 tokens output). We know that's tight.
[00:55] Riley Gomez: Noted. That informs the shortlist — we typically map models to hardware/quant profiles in the compat matrix.
[01:05] Maya Chen: I'll start with the catalog — think of it as a matchmaking layer. We pull open models, run a battery of lightweight bench tests, and produce a compatibility score across dimensions: latency, cost per 1k tokens, accuracy proxy (task-specific), memory footprint, and kernel/quant friendliness.
[01:23] Priya Kapoor: Can you show an example of the compat matrix?
[01:26] Riley Gomez: Sure, pulling up the demo in Console — forgive any screen switching noise. On the left is model metadata, middle columns are bench signals, right is runtime fit guidance. For instance, you can see 'opt-13b-qlora' flagged as high-accuracy but requires a different kernel mapping on older Ampere cards.
[01:45] Tom Boyle: When you say kernel mapping, are we talking about CUDA kernels or something Redwood abstracts?
[01:50] Riley Gomez: Both — we select optimized kernels at runtime. Sometimes a model benefits from a fused attention kernel; other times the quant path is more important. Console shows a recommended kernel profile per model and per hardware family.
[02:05] Jorge Mendes: How do you derive accuracy proxy? We need signal for our QA intents which are more factual recall vs hallucination.
[02:13] Maya Chen: Good question. We take representative prompt sets — you can upload your own — and run a lightweight eval that measures exact-match or ROUGE-like proxies depending on task. For the initial shortlist we usually use a small labeled prompt set to approximate precision/recall.
[02:28] Priya Kapoor: So we feed our prompts and you produce a bench report? Is that part of the pilot?
[02:33] Liam Patel: Yes — for the pilot we ask for 100-200 prompts across the main intents; Riley will run benches across 6-8 candidate models, with configs for hosted and dedicated stacks.
[02:45] Aisha Rahman: Are these benches synthetic or with real PII?
[02:49] Lina Park: Security here — we can't send PII. What are the data handling guarantees if we use hosted?
[02:55] Liam Patel: Good call. Hosted keeps telemetry but we have a business process: we can run the bench in your VPC (Private) or we can scrub inputs. We also have dedicated pools that can be contractually isolated. We'll share SOC2, and KMS integration notes — those go in the security packet.
[03:10] Lina Park: Do you support customer-managed KMS/HSM?
[03:13] Riley Gomez: Yes. For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS and can disable persistence of KV cache to disk if needed. For Dedicated we provide options to isolate and mute telemetry.
[03:23] Jorge Mendes: Back to compat matrix — what about quantization? We care a lot about 4-bit quant for cost.
[03:29] Riley Gomez: The compat matrix shows a quant flag. We mark models as 'quant-friendly' when our internal kernel set preserves quality with int4. There's also a column for 'KV cache memory' which matters for long-context workloads.
[03:42] Priya Kapoor: How often do you refresh the catalog? Models are changing fast.
[03:46] Maya Chen: We refresh weekly for new public releases and re-run the quick bench for any models in the watchlist. For models you pin we keep deterministic profiles and rebench on demand.
[03:55] Tom Boyle: If we pin a model version, can we enforce rollout policies? Canary, rollback?
[03:58] Liam Patel: Yes — Console supports canary rollouts, traffic splits, and automatic fallbacks to lower-cost variants. You can set policies by latency SLO and cost threshold.
[04:10] Jorge Mendes: On the bench side, what metrics should we expect in the report?
[04:13] Riley Gomez: Latency p50/p95/p99, token throughput, cost per 1k tokens (estimates), accuracy proxy by prompt group, memory footprint, and a kernel/quant compatibility note. We'll also include a suggested runtime mapping: e.g., A100-80GB + int8 for model X, L4 or T4 for smaller models, etc.
[04:30] Priya Kapoor: Do you surface per-token billing surprises? We saw other vendors charge for hidden tokens.
[04:34] Maya Chen: Console breaks down billing: input tokens, output tokens, caching hits (we show prefix/KV cache hit rate), and any orchestration overhead. We can generate token-level logs for your billing reconciliation.
[04:45] Lina Park: For compliance, we require audit logs for all inference requests. Can Redwood provide that?
[04:50] Riley Gomez: Yes — we provide audit logs and integrate with SIEMs. For Private deployments you can keep logs inside your VPC.
[04:58] Aisha Rahman: What about on-prem air-gapped?
[05:01] Liam Patel: We offer an on-prem package for regulated workloads, takes longer to provision but meets air-gap constraints, and you control the entire control plane.
[05:10] Jorge Mendes: I'm curious about fallback policies. If a large model becomes overloaded, do you polyglot route to smaller variants automatically?
[05:16] Riley Gomez: Exactly. Smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants; the compat matrix defines compatibility groups so we only route to models with similar prompt-output semantics. You can set constraints — e.g., don't fall back if accuracy falls below X.
[05:28] Priya Kapoor: Nice. Let's flip to a concrete example: QA-assistant. What would your shortlist look like?
[05:32] Riley Gomez: For QA we'd usually start with 3 buckets: high-accuracy LLMs (13B+ qlora/finetuned), mid-tier quant-friendly 7-13B models, and small fast models for caching. We'll run the bench and present a pick with tradeoffs.
[05:44] Jorge Mendes: How do you account for context-window tradeoffs? We have long docs sometimes.
[05:48] Maya Chen: The matrix includes a context-window score and estimated cost for long contexts. For long documents we often recommend prefix caching strategies and reranker + narrow-context retrieval — those are patterns documented in the Console playbook.
[05:58] Tom Boyle: Any SLA commitments on latency for Dedicated?
[06:02] Liam Patel: We offer SLA-backed latency targets for Dedicated tiers; specifics depend on committed capacity. We'll include a proposed SLO in the pilot SOW.
[06:10] Priya Kapoor: Can we see the bench report format?
[06:13] Riley Gomez: Yep — I'll share an example PDF. It has charts for latency distributions, cost curves, and a compatibility heatmap.
[06:19] Jorge Mendes: One more: does the bench simulate batching and real traffic patterns?
[06:23] Riley Gomez: We can run two modes: microbench (single-request latency) and traffic-sim which replays your traffic profile to capture batching behavior. For your pilot we recommend the traffic-sim.
[06:34] Aisha Rahman: If we simulate real traffic, do you need any infra changes?
[06:37] Riley Gomez: No, we can run from Redwood hosted and replay to hosted endpoints, or we can run inside your VPC to avoid sending data out.
[06:45] Priya Kapoor: Security again — what telemetry remains when running in our VPC?
[06:49] Liam Patel: In VPC Private mode telemetry is optional and can be configured. For Dedicated we can also limit telemetry to aggregated metrics only. We'll document that.
[06:58] Lina Park: We'll need to review your SOC2 and the exact KMS flow. Also we need to know where KV cache is persisted.
[07:05] Riley Gomez: KV cache persisted to memory by default, but can be configured to not persist to disk. We support in-memory only caches and can flush on shutdown.
[07:14] Tom Boyle: For our SREs, how do we debug a kernel mismatch in production?
[07:18] Riley Gomez: Console includes tracing hooks and per-request trace IDs, with kernel selection logs. You can also set a flag to force a kernel choice for an instance.
[07:27] Jorge Mendes: Pricing — ballpark numbers for hosted vs dedicated?
[07:31] Liam Patel: I'll send a tailored estimate after we see your traffic profile, but rough rule: hosted is faster to start and flexible; dedicated gives 30-50% unit cost savings for steady traffic, especially when combined with quant and caching. We'll include estimates in the SOW.
[07:45] Priya Kapoor: Sounds good. What's the proposed timeline to pilot?
[07:48] Liam Patel: We suggested a pilot next week: 2-hour bench run + 1-day analysis. If we get your prompts and traffic profile by Friday (2025-10-10) we can run the traffic-sim next Tue/Wed.
[07:59] Jorge Mendes: We can get prompts to you Friday.
[08:02] Aisha Rahman: We'll also need an architecture diagram for Dedicated and Private.
[08:06] Liam Patel: We'll include that in the security packet.
[08:10] Riley Gomez: Back to catalog nuance — compatibility groups: we group models by semantic similarity using a combination of embedding-space distances and bench-task concordance. This helps avoid routing to a model that produces a different style or hallucination profile.
[08:26] Priya Kapoor: Any examples of where routing hurt because of semantics?
[08:29] Riley Gomez: Yes — we had a customer where a summarization model was routed to a chat-optimized variant and the outputs became verbose. The compat matrix caught that and we enforced routing to the summarization group.
[08:40] Jorge Mendes: Does Console let us annotate models? We want to tag some models as 'approved for prod only after manual review'.
[08:45] Maya Chen: Yes — tags and approval gates exist. You can lock models so they don't auto-update and require approver sign-off.
[08:53] Tom Boyle: What about A/B evaluate? We want to test two models in prod under a controlled experiment.
[08:58] Riley Gomez: Built-in A/B routing and quality observability. We can tie evaluation metrics to prompt sets and run significance tests.
[09:08] Priya Kapoor: Great. Let's talk about what you'll share after this call.
[09:12] Liam Patel: We'll send: 1) Security packet (SOC2, KMS notes, architecture diagrams), 2) Example bench report and compat matrix CSV, 3) Short pilot SOW with pricing estimates, 4) Link to Console demo tenant with a sample catalog.
[09:23] Lina Park: Please include exact data flow diagrams for hosted vs private.
[09:26] Liam Patel: Will do.
[09:28] Jorge Mendes: One last technical: how do you handle tokenizer differences across model variants when comparing accuracy?
[09:33] Riley Gomez: We normalize tokenization by using a canonical tokenizer step per model and do overlap-aware scoring. It's not perfect but adequate as a proxy; we recommend final evaluation at full-fidelity during the pilot.
[09:44] Aisha Rahman: For the pilot, will you simulate on the same hardware we intend to use? We're leaning towards A100 clouds and possibly an on-prem L4 cluster for inference.
[09:52] Riley Gomez: We can match the hardware in the bench: A100, H100, L4 — we annotate results per hardware in the report. If you're evaluating on-prem L4 we can map kernels and quant paths accordingly.
[10:05] Priya Kapoor: Anything else we should know about hidden costs?
[10:09] Maya Chen: Watch for cold-starts and memory overhead for KV caches — both can show up as transient costs. Our Optimize toolkit recommends cache TTLs and batching configs to minimize those.
[10:20] Jorge Mendes: How does Optimize provide batching suggestions?
[10:23] Riley Gomez: Optimize analyzes request distributions and suggests batch sizes and concurrent worker counts to reach latency SLOs with minimal cost. It's in Console as a report, and we can apply recommended configs to a Dedicated pool automatically if you want.
[10:36] Tom Boyle: Do you support custom autoscaling policies?
[10:39] Liam Patel: Yes — autoscaling policies can be based on p95 latency, queue length, or GPU utilization, and you can set min/max capacity and burst windows.
[10:48] Priya Kapoor: Time check — we're at about 34 minutes. Aisha, Lina any last security blockers?
[10:54] Lina Park: Not blockers, but we need the SOC2 and the KMS flow chart. Also need to confirm audit log retention controls.
[11:02] Liam Patel: We'll include retention config options; you can set retention windows per environment.
[11:06] Jorge Mendes: Ok, next practical steps. We'll deliver prompts and traffic profile by 2025-10-10, you run traffic-sim next week, and deliver bench report + matrix within 48 hours of run.
[11:17] Liam Patel: Affirmative. I'll send a calendar invite for the pilot run once we confirm the data.
[11:22] Priya Kapoor: Sounds good.
[11:24] Riley Gomez: Any competitor concerns? We hear you might be talking to Bedrock; our difference is the unified Console + Optimize toolkit and the fallback routing semantics.
[11:35] Priya Kapoor: Yes we're also evaluating Bedrock for marketplace convenience.
[11:38] Liam Patel: Understood. We'll focus the pilot on measurable latency/cost and the compat matrix so you can compare apples-to-apples.
[11:45] Aisha Rahman: Quick question for the SREs — is there an ops runbook when a kernel fails or out-of-memory occurs?
[11:50] Riley Gomez: Yes — Console provides incident steps, safe-fallback toggles, and a 'drain last N' feature so you can remove pods without losing KV state.
[11:58] Priya Kapoor: Alright, wrapping up. Recap of next steps?
[12:02] Liam Patel: Recap: Arsenal to send prompts + traffic profile by 2025-10-10; Redwood (Riley + Liam) to run traffic-sim pilot next week and deliver bench report + compatibility matrix; Redwood to send security packet and pilot SOW; schedule follow-up review within 48 hours of report.
[12:18] Priya Kapoor: Thanks all. We'll get the artifacts over and review the security packet asap.
[12:23] Liam Patel: Appreciate your time. We'll follow up with the links and invite.
[12:27] Meeting end.
